newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea seen easing bank reserve ratio - analysts.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea seen easing bank reserve ratio - analysts.

text.p: South Korea is expected to unveil plans to boost the nation's ailing economy on Wednesday, possibly driving down bank interest rates for the second time this year, analysts said on Tuesday.

Stock prices surged this week on expectations the government would announce measures to cut the reserve requirement for banks by an average of two percent at an economic ministers' meeting on Wednesday, the analysts said.
Any cut in the reserve requirements ratio is expected to be swiftly followed by cuts in bank lending rates.
"The ratio cut is a policy direction. It's a matter of timing," said Lee Seung-hun, a banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

President Kim Young-sam will chair Wednesday's meeting, where officials will discuss ways to help South Korean companies become more competitive as a steady slide in exports continues to hammer away at profit margins.

Analysts said lowering reserve requirements was in line with South Korea's efforts to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), whose members typically keep reserve requirements in a zero to three percent range.

South Korea, which wants to join the OECD this year, in April trimmed the requirement ratio -- the average proportion of total deposits banks must place as reserves with the central bank -- to 7.4 percent from 9.4 percent previously.
Banks responded quickly, lowering lending rates by an average of 0.22 percentage points.

"As far as I'm concerned, the central bank and the finance ministry have agreed in principle to reduce the rate. But they are still discussing ways to soak up increasing liquidity," said Yoon Yong-chul, banking analyst at Daewoo Securities.
The government has declined to comment on any plans to cut the reserve requirement. A finance ministry official said on Tuesday: "We cannot comment on the market speculation at this stage."

"Although it's not officially confirmed, many investors hope the government will cut the rate one way or another," said Hwang Chang-joong, analyst at LG Securities, referring to comments by President Kim that South Korea needed measures to cure its economic ills of high costs and low efficiency.
